summary:
The model is supported in vLLM, welcome to try this powerful model on your own🚀
Quoting @ArtificialAnlys
MiniMax launches their first reasoning model: MiniMax M1, the second most intelligent open weights model after DeepSeek R1, with a much longer 1M token context window
@minimax_ai M1 is based on their Text-01 model (released 14 Jan 2025) - an MoE with 456B total and 45.9B active parameters. This makes M1’s total parameter count smaller than DeepSeek R1’s 671B total parameters but larger than Qwen3 235B-A22B. Both Text-01 and M1 only support text input and output.
MiniMax M1 80K scores 63 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. This lags DeepSeek R1 0528, but is slightly ahead of Alibaba’s Qwen3 235B-A22B and NVIDIA’s Llama 3.1 Nemotron Ultra. MiniMax M1 is offered in two variants: M1 40K and M1 80K, offering 40k and 80k token thinking budgets respectively.
MiniMax discloses that their full RL training on Text-01 to create M1 used 512 H800 GPUs for three weeks - equivalent to a rental cost of $0.53M. This number is an interesting datapoint for the current degree of scaling of reinforcement learning. We note that it is not comparable to DeepSeek’s famous $5.6M training cost claim for DeepSeek V3, as DeepSeek’s number referred to full pre-training of the model not the reinforcement learning step.
MiniMax offers models across multiple modalities on their Talkie app and API, including their Artificial Analysis Speech Leaderboard topping Speech-02 model, and Video models (T2V-01, and I2V-01). MiniMax M1 is the first of five announcements in their MiniMax Week.
Availability:
➤ MiniMax M1 is available via MiniMax’s first-party API, priced at $0.4/$2.1 per 1M input/output tokens for ≤200k input tokens. The price increases to $1.2/$2.1 per 1M input/output tokens for >200k input tokens
➤ M1 is also currently available on @Novita, priced at $0.55/$2.2 per 1M input/output tokens with a 128k token context window
➤ M1 40k and M1 80k are both open weights models released under the Apache 2.0 license and we expect to see more third-party APIs supporting these models

llm-compressor v0.6.0 is out. Big improvements for anyone optimizing models for inference with @vllm_project.
1⃣ AWQ now works better for MoEs, with major runtime gains.
2⃣Calibration is faster and smoother with sequential on-loading. This cuts runtime and reduces hardware needs for large models.
3⃣Better memory handling when offloading to CPUs, no more "out of memory" crashes
4⃣Early FP4 support (NVFP4) is here, fully integrated with vLLM for non-MoE models
If you are scaling LLM inference, this release means faster compression, smaller models, and lower costs.

summary:
Random Samples, our weekly seminar series that bridges the gap between cutting-edge AI research and real-world application, continue this Friday, July 18!
Title:
Grounding Feedback is All You Need: Aligning Small Vision-Language Models
Abstract:
While recent vision-language models (VLMs) excel at integrating visual and linguistic information, their performance hinges on vast quantities of curated image-text pairs. This reliance makes the alignment process both time-consuming and resource-intensive. In this talk, we'll introduce Sampling-Based Vision Projection (SVP), a novel framework that improves vision-language alignment using automated feedback and minimal human supervision. Our results show that SVP significantly enhances image captioning, improves object recall, and reduces hallucination, enabling smaller models to match the performance of much larger systems. This approach offers a promising path toward developing powerful, efficient, and accessible multimodal AI.

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
2. Prefill and Decode Disaggregation
In long-context or decode-heavy generation, contention between prefill and decode slows everything down.
llm-d now lets you disaggregate these stages across nodes. Each is scheduled independently for better latency and GPU efficiency.
You get better utilization and fewer stalls. And it works within Kubernetes-native orchestration, using our updated deployment patterns and profiling tools.
How much does disaggregation help in practice?
Here’s a Pareto curve for Llama-Scout on two 8xH200 nodes with Infiniband. We compare a monolithic 4tp4 topology to a disaggregated 4ptp2–2dtp4 setup, using the same GPU count.
(Detailed and clear explanation of the chart are in the release blog that's linked at the end of this thread)

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
We're thrilled to share an integration between KServe and @_llm_d_, bringing powerful, scalable LLM serving to @kubernetesio.
Our @RedHatAI team is integrating llm-d, a Kubernetes-native distributed inference framework, into KServe. This is all about combining the best of both worlds: KServe's rich ecosystem and llm-d's scalable, performance-first architecture.
Here’s a snapshot of our recent progress:
☑️ New LLMInference CRD for a consistent API
☑️ Reconciliation Logic to ensure deployments are always correct
☑️ Production-ready w/ GIE EPP & InferencePool for running LLMs at scale
☑️ Support for multiple storage backends (S3, PVC, OCI)
☑️ End-to-end encryption for securityThis integration creates a more robust, production-grade LLM serving experience.
A big thank you to everyone in the community who helped make this happen! Stay tuned for the next release.

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
This is the main topic at tomorrow's virtual vLLM office hours! We'll share the three latest features in LLM Compressor v0.7.0:
1. Transform-based modifiers, a new approach to decreasing quantization loss without need of a calibration dataset or significant compute time.
2. Non-uniform quantization, so that users have more flexibility and control in setting precision in each layer of the model.
3. Support for block-quantization, as found in DeepSeek v3.
Join to find out how it works, how it can be run in llm-compressor, and next steps to benchmark performance against AWQ, GPTQ and round-to-nearest on a wide range of models.

I covered:
* Basics of inference engine flow (input/output request processing, scheduling, paged attention, continuous batching)

* Scaling up: going from smaller LMs that can be hosted on a single GPU all the way to trillion+ params (via TP/PP/SP) -> multi-GPU, multi-node setup
* Serving the model on the web: going from offline deployment to multiple API servers, load balancing, DP coordinator, multiple engines setup :)
* Measuring perf of inference systems (latency (ttft, itl, e2e, tpot), throughput) and GPU perf roofline model
Lots of examples, lots of visuals!

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
New blog: Scaling DeepSeek-style MoEs with vLLM + llm-d using Wide EP
Sparse MoE models replace dense MLP layers with hundreds of “experts.” Only a few experts in each layer activate per token (top-k routing), allowing models like DeepSeek V3 to scale massively without proportional compute.
But scaling MoE introduces real challenges: inefficient dispatch/combine kernels, memory overhead, communication bottlenecks across GPUs/nodes, and uneven expert usage.
How vLLM helps:
• Expert + data parallelism for MoE layers
• Optimized sparse dispatch/combine kernels
• Expert Parallel Load Balancer (EPLB) to rebalance skewed usage
• Prefill vs decode disaggregation to handle long-context prompts efficiently
How llm-d extends into production:
• Kubernetes-native inference orchestration
• Prefix/KV-cache aware routing and intelligent scheduling
• Multi-node expert parallelism with optimized communication (DeepEP/PPLX/NVSHMEM)
• Validated “well-lit paths” for distributed MoE deployments and for prefill-decode disaggregation, which is critical for large-scale Wide EP serving
The result: vLLM + llm-d make today’s largest sparse MoE models, including DeepSeek V3 and similar architectures, deployable at scale, balancing latency, resource efficiency, and production readiness.

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
🚀 Big news! The September '25 batch of Red Hat AI Validated Models is here! Our goal is to give you the confidence, predictability, and flexibility you need to deploy third-party generative AI models across the Red Hat AI platform.
Why do you need validated models?
Selecting the right LLM for your use case is hard. Enterprises often struggle with:
🤯 Model selection complexity
⚖️ AI resource planning
📉 Ensuring performance can be reliably reproduced
You can't "guess" your way into production.
That's where Red Hat AI's model validation process comes in. We simplify the selection by performing extensive testing for you:
📊 Performance Benchmarking (w/ GuideLLM)
✅ Accuracy Evaluations (w/ LM Evaluation Harness)
🔄 Reproducible Deployments (on vLLM)
This provides clear capacity planning guidance for customers before they go to production.
Now, meet the September '25 lineup, a diverse batch optimized for your enterprise workloads:
· Kimi K2 Quantized INT4: A RAG powerhouse. Its massive context window is built for analyzing lengthy documents, like legal contracts or research papers. See it on Hugging Face:
· Gemma-3n 4B FP8 Dynamic: Google's next-gen efficient model. Perfect for summarization and on-device tasks. See it on Hugging Face:
· DeepSeek-R1 INT4: An elite coding model for generating, completing, and debugging complex code. See it on Hugging Face:
· Qwen 3 8B FP8 Dynamic: A versatile and powerful multilingual model from Alibaba Cloud, ideal for global chatbots and content creation. See it on Hugging Face:
Get started today. You can run these models now on Red Hat Inference Server v3.2.1 and Red Hat OpenShift AI v2.24.
In addition to Hugging Face, you can also access them as container images from the Red Hat Container Registry. They'll also be in the RHOAI Model catalog (coming in November😉)!
Stay tuned for the next batch of validated models coming next month, including models like gpt-oss and Qwen3-Coder.

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
The llm-d community just dropped a deep dive on prefix cache aware scheduling. It explains how:
▫️ vLLM’s prefix caching works under the hood
▫️ Naive schedulers waste cache hits in distributed setups
▫️ llm-d’s cache-aware scheduling does things differently (using KVEvents + cache affinity scoring)
The work shows real-world implications for multi-tenant inference and throughput scaling. The surprising part isn’t just that it fixes inefficiencies; it’s the magnitude of the effect. In benchmarks, the team saw…
…up to 57x faster response times vs. approximate scheduling, and 2x higher throughput compared to cache-blind baselines.
A great example of how careful systems design translates theory into production performance. Huge thanks to contributors across @IBMResearch, @RedHat, @GoogleAI, @alibaba_cloud, and DaoCloud who made this work happen.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G1ySppZawAAm06p.jpg

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
How does @deepseek_ai Sparse Attention (DSA) work?
It has 2 components: the Lightning Indexer and Sparse Multi-Latent Attention (MLA). The indexer keeps a small key cache of 128 per token (vs. 512 for MLA). It scores incoming queries. The top-2048 tokens to pass to Sparse MLA.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2AbP5KaAAAkhTP.jpg

✨ Built on V3.1-Terminus, it debuts DeepSeek Sparse Attention(DSA) for faster, more efficient training & inference on long context.

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
.@_llm_d_ v0.3 is out and delivers major upgrades for scalable, hardware-agnostic inference.
What’s new:
• Expanded hardware support, including Google TPU + Intel XPU
• TCP & RDMA over RoCE disaggregation
• A predicted latency based balancing preview that improves P90 latency by up to 3x in long-prefill workloads
• Wide expert parallel (EP) scaling to 2.2k tokens per second per H200 GPU
• Inference Gateway (IGW) v1.0 GA
• KV disaggregation, adaptive SLO predictor, observability via Grafana + ServiceMonitor, curated guides for GKE, OpenShift, CoreWeave, DigitalOcean
Taken together, these results redefine the operating envelope for inference. llm-d enables clusters to run hotter before scaling out, extracting more value from each GPU, and still meet strict latency objectives. The result is a control plane built not just for speed, but for predictable, cost-efficient scale.
Full details:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G3Oc0uRXAAA0kPE.jpg

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
BIG NEWS! 🎉 Compressed Tensors is officially joining the @vllm_project!
Built on top of the excellent @huggingface safetensors framework, Compressed Tensors extends it with efficient storage and management of compressed tensor data for model quantization and sparsity.
Why Compressed Tensors?
As model compression becomes key to efficient LLM deployment, the landscape of quantization techniques has grown fragmented, each with its own format and loading procedure. Compressed Tensors solves this with a single, extensible format that supports a wide variety of compression schemes.
What does it offer?
1⃣ Unified checkpoint format across compression methods
2⃣ Broad compatibility with GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, SparseGPT, FP8, NVFP4, and more
3⃣ Flexible quantization formats: weight-only, weight+activation, KV-cache, attention, mixed (non-uniform)
4⃣ Sparsity support for both unstructured and semi-structured (e.g., 2:4) schemes
5⃣ Seamless integration with @huggingface Transformers, @PyTorch, and @vllm_project
🔗

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
Welcome! 🥰
Quoting @RedHat_AI
BIG NEWS! 🎉 Compressed Tensors is officially joining the @vllm_project!
Built on top of the excellent @huggingface safetensors framework, Compressed Tensors extends it with efficient storage and management of compressed tensor data for model quantization and sparsity.
Why Compressed Tensors?
As model compression becomes key to efficient LLM deployment, the landscape of quantization techniques has grown fragmented, each with its own format and loading procedure. Compressed Tensors solves this with a single, extensible format that supports a wide variety of compression schemes.
What does it offer?
1⃣ Unified checkpoint format across compression methods
2⃣ Broad compatibility with GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, SparseGPT, FP8, NVFP4, and more
3⃣ Flexible quantization formats: weight-only, weight+activation, KV-cache, attention, mixed (non-uniform)
4⃣ Sparsity support for both unstructured and semi-structured (e.g., 2:4) schemes
5⃣ Seamless integration with @huggingface Transformers, @PyTorch, and @vllm_project
🔗

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
🔥 New Blog: “Disaggregated Inference: 18 Months Later”
18 months in LLM inference feels like a new Moore’s Law cycle – but this time not just 2x per year:
💸 Serving cost ↓10–100x
🚀 Throughput ↑10x
⚡ Latency ↓5x
A big reason? Disaggregated Inference.
From DistServe, our early research system on prefill-decode disaggregation, to today’s production frameworks, disaggregation has become the backbone of modern LLM serving.
So what is disaggregated inference?
Why does the LLM inference community love it?
And how far have we come?
As the inventors of this technique, we take a look back – 18 months later - at how the idea reshaped the landscape and what comes next.
🔗 Read the full story:

linked_urls.title: Disaggregated Inference: 18 Months Later | Hao AI Lab @ UCSD
linked_urls.summary: Eighteen months ago, our lab introduced DistServe with a simple bet: split LLM inference into prefill and decode, and scale them independently on separate compute pools. Today, almost every production-grade LLM serving framework – NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d, Ray Serve LLM SGLang, vLLM, LMCache, MoonCake – runs on disaggregation and demonstrates its power in large-scale, real-world LLM serving workloads, with many more continuing to push its boundaries. Concepts like TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TPOT (time-per-output-token), now standard latency metrics in nearly every serving benchmark, were also popularized through the lens of disaggregation.

If you built agents with Llama Stack's original Agent APIs, you've probably seen that they are being deprecated in favor of the OpenAI compatible Responses API.
Migrating does not require starting over.
There are two practical paths you can take.
Approach 1 is a straightforward rewrite. Move directly to the Responses API and simplify your agent logic with a single call that handles reasoning, tool planning, and output generation. This gives you a cleaner architecture and reduces complexity.
Approach 2 is an emulation layer. If you want to preserve your existing structure, you can wrap your legacy patterns around the Responses API. This maintains compatibility while unlocking the new capabilities.

That means day-0 support for new models, and spec decoding for anyone who can’t train.
Quoting @RedHat_AI
Speculative decoding is a powerful way to improve inference performance, but in practice it has been hard to adopt.
Training a unique draft model per LLM is time-consuming, and production-ready training utilities that work cleanly with vLLM have been limited.
Speculators v0.3.0 closes this gap with end-to-end training support for Eagle3 draft models that run seamlessly with vLLM.
The release adds offline data generation using vLLM and training support for single and multi-layer draft models, across both MoE and non-MoE verifiers.

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
Scaling MoE inference is often communication + KV-cache bound: once you push expert parallelism, decode can become dominated by collectives and imbalance, and prefill stragglers can stall an entire EP group.
New community benchmark results for vLLM wide-EP on multi-node H200 (Coreweave, Infiniband + ConnectX-7):
- Sustained ~2.2k tokens/s per H200 GPU (up from earlier ~1.5k tokens/s per GPU)
In the post we share the key pieces that enable this:
- Wide-EP (`--enable-expert-parallel`) for DeepSeek-style MoE + MLA KV efficiency
- DeepEP all-to-all, Dual-batch Overlap (DBO), and Expert Parallel Load Balancing (EPLB)
- Prefill/Decode disaggregation and deployment paths via llm-d, NVIDIA Dynamo, and Ray Serve LLM
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/G8dxCDrakAEgqKm.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/tweet_video/G8dxCDrakAEgqKm.mp4

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
Cohere shared a strong production case study during recent @vllm_project office hours on how they use LLM Compressor and the AWQ compression algorithm to make large MoE models deployable.
Their focus is private, on-prem deployments where GPUs and cost are tightly constrained. Many Cohere models use Mixture-of-Experts architectures, which significantly increases inference-time memory. Without 4-bit weight quantization, these models would be impractical to deploy.
LLM Compressor enables fast exploration of quantization strategies through adaptable algorithms, non-uniform quantization across layers, and seamless integration with vLLM for rapid iteration.
A key challenge was calibration. Using standard datasets degraded performance on long-context agentic tasks inside North, Cohere's enterprise AI platform. Analysis showed failures were driven by repetitive chat templates and tool descriptions biasing AWQ statistics.
By adding token masking support to AWQ in LLM Compressor, Cohere eliminated that bias and produced production-ready 4-bit models that met their quality bar.
As hardware evolved, Cohere extended AWQ from INT4 W4A16 to NVFP4 W4A16 for Blackwell GPUs, and observed meaningful speedups with W4A8 for compute-bound workloads. Dense and MoE W4A8 serving is supported in vLLM today.
This is a great example of why LLM Compressor matters for real systems, not just benchmarks.
Huge thanks to Zewen Shen, Ali Edalati, Bharat Venkitesh, and the team at @cohere for sharing this work, and to the @RedHat AI team for their hard work on making LLM Compressor a production-grade model optimization library.
P.S. Both Cohere and Red Hat are hiring! If you want to work on efficient AI, reply to this post and we'll get in touch.

summary:
For many engineers, we can remember the first time we tried AI coding assistants. Trust me, it’s come a LONG way! But now, with agentic coding tools like #ClaudeCode, #Cursor, and #Codex, how can you get the results you need from an LLM without spending all your time going back and forth about a wrong dependency or missing test cases 😆
You might’ve tried “vibe coding” by letting the model suggest edits, but there’s one common issue: *why* did the model take the action it did? That’s why spec coding, or using a set of specifications and a design document, has gotten incredibly popular recently. You not only get to use an LLM to improve productivity, but also keep Software Delivery Lifecycle (SDLC) components that are super important!
My friends at @IBM just helped me put together a quick lightboard on the topic, and I’d love it if you checked it out! Cheers :)

summary:
FlashAttention 3 has ~70,000 lines of code. The vLLM Triton attention backend has ~800.
On H100 it hits 100.7% of FlashAttention 3 performance. On AMD MI300 it delivers a 5.8x speedup over earlier implementations. Same kernel source code on both.
IBM Research, Red Hat, and AMD built this for vLLM to solve the portability problem: one kernel, any GPU vendor.
Check it out 👇
Quoting @vllm_project
Maintaining separate attention kernels for every GPU platform doesn't scale.
The vLLM Triton attention backend takes a different approach: ~800 lines of Triton, same source code across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs. On H100, it matches state-of-the-art attention performance. On MI300, ~5.8x faster than earlier implementations.
The blog covers Q blocks for better dot utilization, parallel tiled softmax for decode, persistent kernels for CUDA graph compatibility, and cross-platform benchmarking.
Now the default attention backend on AMD ROCm, also available on NVIDIA and Intel.

Thanks to @IBMResearch, @RedHat_AI, and @AIatAMD for driving this work!

GPU-only inference collapses once HBM saturates. @_llm_d_ v0.5 is built for what happens after that.
New: hierarchical KV offloading (GPU → CPU → disk) sustains ~185k tok/s where GPU-only falls off a cliff. 13.9x improvement at 250 concurrent users.
Also shipping: scale-to-zero for idle workloads, LoRA-aware cache routing, UCCL networking with 2.4x better congestion resilience, and reproducible benchmarks for every performance claim.

Your agent works on your laptop. But does it have identity? Isolation? Audit trails? Observability with agent tracing? Can you prove to compliance what tools it called and why?
Most teams can't.

Quoting @vllm_project
Training spec decoding drafters (Eagle-3, P-Eagle…) needs verifier hidden states. Previously that meant using transformers (losing vLLM optimizations) or heavy-patching vLLM internals.
vLLM (v0.18.0+) now extracts hidden states natively, reusing Eagle-3 pathways + KV Connector API. Prefix caching, chunked prefill, paged memory all work out of the box.

I have been writing a small series on LLM inference with @vllm_project that can be a practical starting point for people trying to understand this space.
Along with the explanations, I also ran benchmarks on realistic workloads across different GPUs and datasets to evaluate how these techniques perform in practice.
It covers:
- Major speculative decoding techniques
- Major quantization methods
- Distributed inference: DP / PP / TP
- Expert Parallelism and mixed parallel setups
- Practical optimization techniques like prefix caching, KV cache, and disaggregated prefill/decode
My goal was to explain how these techniques work, where they help, so it is easier to choose the right approach for a given workload.
This series is useful not only for people getting into LLM serving, but also for engineers who are already serving LLMs and want to optimize inference, improve throughput, reduce latency, or evaluate the right serving strategy.

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
🎉 Day-0 support for @deepseek_ai V4 Pro and Flash on vLLM — a new generation of DeepSeek model, purpose-built for tasks up to 1M tokens. Alongside the release, we're publishing a first-principles walkthrough of the new long-context attention and how we implemented it in vLLM.
The new attention mechanism, in four moves:
• Shared K/V + inverse RoPE → 2× memory savings
• c4a / c128a KV compression → 4×–128× savings
• DeepSeek Sparse Attention over compressed tokens
• Short sliding window for locality across compression boundaries
At 1M context, per-layer KV state is ~8.7× smaller than a DeepSeek V3.2-style 61-layer stack (9.62 GiB vs 83.9 GiB, bf16). fp8 attention cache + fp4 indexer cache shrink it further.
vLLM side:
• Unified hybrid KV cache — single logical block size (256 native positions) across all compression rates; compressor state folded into the SWA KV cache spec so prefix caching, disagg prefill, CUDA graphs and MTP reuse the same abstraction
• Three page-size buckets for the full 5-way cache stack → no cross-kind fragmentation
• Fused kernels: compressor + RMSNorm + RoPE + cache insert (1.4–3×), inverse RoPE + fp8 quant (2–3×), Q-norm + KV RoPE + K insert (10–20×)
• Multi-stream overlap of indexer vs main-KV compression vs SWA insertion
Disaggregated serving is supported out of the box and strongly recommended for best performance.
Follow our recipes site for verified commands for @nvidia Blackwell (B200, B300, GB200, GB300) and Hopper (H100/H200/H20) systems.
Thanks to the @deepseek_ai team for open-sourcing DeepSeek V4, and to @inferact for landing day-0 support 🤝

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
summary:
Speculators v0.5.0 is out. Two big additions:
1. DFlash training support. Unlike Eagle 3, which generates draft tokens autoregressively, DFlash uses block diffusion to generate an entire block in a single forward pass. Better ITL. Gemma 4 DFlash hits 4.91 mean acceptance length on HumanEval, 5.17 on math reasoning.
2. Online training, for the first time. Train directly on hidden states generated on-the-fly. No pre-caching needed.
Both now run through @vllm_project's native hidden states extraction system, introduced in v0.18.0.
Full release notes:

RAG systems rank by relevance, not authorization. A query from one tenant can surface another tenant's data simply because it scores highest.
Red Hat's @franciscojarceo co-authored a paper on fixing this.
MLOps Community, June 11, 1:30 PM EDT (virtual)

linked_urls.title: Securing the Agent: Vendor-Neutral, Multitenant Enterprise Retrieval and Tool Use - Event | MLOps Community
linked_urls.summary: Paper: Securing the Agent: Vendor-Neutral, Multitenant Enterprise Retrieval and Tool UseRetrieval-Augmented Generation and agentic AI are increasingly common in enterprise deployments, but real enterprise environments introduce challenges largely absent from academic treatments and consumer-facing APIs: multiple tenants with heterogeneous data, strict access-control requirements, regulatory compliance, and cost pressures that demand shared infrastructure. This paper identifies a fundamental problem underlying existing RAG architectures in these settings. Retrieval systems rank documents by relevance, not by authorization, so a query from one tenant can surface another tenant’s confidential data simply because it scores highest. The authors formalize this relevance-authorization gap alongside related shortcomings (tool-mediated disclosure, context accumulation across turns, client-side orchestration bypass) and introduce a layered isolation architecture combining policy-aware ingestion, retrieval-time gating, and shared inference, enforced through server-side orchestration. They validate it through an open-source implementation in OGX, a vendor-neutral OpenAI-compatible Responses API, showing empirically that ABAC gating eliminates cross-tenant leakage while introducing negligible overhead.The discussion will be led by Francisco Javier Arceo, co-author of the paper, joined by co-hosts David DeStefano, Rohan Prasad, and Valdimar Eggertsson, and moderated by Arthur Coleman. They will walk through the problem, the architecture, and the benchmarks, dig into the open-source framework, and open up to a live audience Q&A.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

clean_title: Elastic Expert Parallelism enables live scaling of vLLM MoE deployments
summary:
A vLLM MoE deployment's DP/EP topology used to be locked in at launch — scaling or swapping config meant a full restart, in-flight traffic dropped. Elastic Expert Parallelism changes that. One API call resizes a live deployment:
curl -X POST localhost:8000/scale_elastic_ep \
-d '{"new_data_parallel_size": 16}'
Under the hood: standby comm groups span the target topology, EPLB redistributes experts across the new EP group, and weights are transferred directly between GPUs over NVIDIA NVLink/RDMA. The same runtime reconfiguration path is what fault-tolerant serving needs: evict failed ranks, redistribute their experts, bring replacements back, no restart.
Thanks to @NVIDIAAI, Sky Computing, @anyscalecompute, @RedHat_AI, and the community.
📖
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI4SH66boAAloRA.jpg
clean_summary: A vLLM MoE deployment's DP/EP topology was previously fixed at launch, requiring a full restart to scale or change configuration, which caused traffic drops. Elastic Expert Parallelism allows resizing a live deployment with a single API call, redistributing experts across GPUs over NVIDIA NVLink/RDMA without restart. This dynamic reconfiguration supports fault-tolerance by evicting failed ranks, redistributing experts, and replacing them seamlessly. The approach is made possible through standby communication groups, expert redistribution, and direct GPU weight transfer, thanks to collaboration with NVIDIA AI, Sky Computing, Anyscale, and Red Hat AI.

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
clean_title: Course on efficient serving of large language models with vLLM
summary:
New course on serving LLMs efficiently -- how do you serve models to many concurrent users at low latency and reasonable cost? This short course is built with @RedHat and taught by @cedricclyburn.
Efficient LLM serving requires efficient memory management. A 70B-parameter model takes ~140 GB just to load the weights. On top of that, every active request needs its own chunk of GPU memory, the KV cache, to store the token context it has built up so far. In this course, you'll learn to reduce a model's memory footprint with quantization and serve it using vLLM, which handles many concurrent requests efficiently through smart memory management.
Skills you'll gain:
- Quantize a model and measure the accuracy tradeoff
- Serve a model with vLLM and watch it handle concurrent requests efficiently
- Benchmark your deployment and make informed tradeoffs between speed, cost, and accuracy
Join and learn to serve LLMs efficiently:
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2062575240027516928/img/UjEluXE3WGYGvkBD.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2062575240027516928/vid/avc1/480x270/rBeB4zTpWGDwH3xt.mp4?tag=27

title: Red Hat AI (@RedHat_AI)
clean_title: Kagenti’s approach to multi-agent security for AI agents
summary:
Multi-agent systems have a hard security problem: Agent A holds a bearer token and passes work to Agent D. Agent D was never supposed to touch patient records. But it can, because the token traveled with the request.
That's a confused deputy. And your audit logs show nothing but normal authorized activity.
Kagenti fixes this at the infrastructure level. Every request carries the full delegation chain, cryptographically signed. Policy fires on the chain, not just the token.
Watch and try it yourself (link in reply):
clean_summary:
Multi-agent systems face a hard security problem: when a request passes through multiple agents, the bearer token can travel with it, potentially allowing agents to access data they shouldn't. This creates a confused deputy scenario, where audit logs may show normal activity despite a security breach.

Kagenti addresses this at the infrastructure level by carrying the full delegation chain in every request, cryptographically signed. Policies then evaluate the entire chain, not just a single token, to enforce correct permissions. You can watch a demonstration of this approach in the linked video.
